Pollytics

By: Beth Neale | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A missing African grey sparks a legal tug-of-war in Mbombela, raising big questions about ownership, animal welfare, and the blurred line between pet and family.

Unique Selling Point:
Human story with a twist: A heartfelt custody battle where the “child” is an African grey parrot – an emotional, relatable story wrapped in an unexpected premise.

Timely legal angle: One of South Africa’s first animal custody disputes to reach the High Court, testing how ownership, possession, and animal welfare intersect in law.

Emotional and visual impact: Genuine footage of Crystle’s final moments with her parrot, strong characters on both sides, and a visually rich contrast between courtroom formality and vibrant bird life.

Broader relevance: Opens discussion on the welfare and intelligence of African greys, a species both endangered and traded, exploring how we define family and responsibility toward sentient animals.

Carte Blanche fit: Balances wit, heart, and investigation – a distinctive story that is topical, emotional, and uniquely South African.

Summary:
BRIEF OVERVIEW:

In Mbombela, a missing parrot story takes flight — and lands in court.

After searching for her beloved African grey for over a year, Crystle Pachos finally finds her bird, Zazu. But her relief is short-lived: another family insists the same African grey, named Zippy, belongs to them. What begins as a touching reunion soon unravels into a full-blown custody case — and a national debate about ownership, attachment, and what it means when an animal is considered “property” under the law.

Pollytics examines this extraordinary story with wit, warmth, and curiosity. Through one parrot’s tale, we explore the intelligence, emotional capacity, and vulnerability of African greys — a species capable of speech, memory, and affection, yet too often misunderstood and mishandled.

With interviews from both families, welfare advocates at Cheeky Beaks, and legal experts, this insert goes beyond the custody fight to examine the broader plight of African greys — one of the world’s most trafficked and misunderstood birds.

It’s a courtroom drama with wings, a love story with feathers, and a reminder that sometimes the loudest truths don’t come from people at all.

LONGER OVERVIEW:

In Mbombela, an unusual custody battle has taken flight — over an African grey parrot.
Crystle Pachos’s parrot, Zazu, disappeared in May 2021. For over a year she searched and waited, convinced he was out there somewhere. On 10 May 2021, she got a tip that a grey had been found. Two days later she went to see the bird and believed immediately that it was Zazu. On 13 May, she had him microchipped, certain her family was whole again.
But at the very same time, another family was living through the same heartbreak. Obert Ntuli, a lawyer, says his parrot Zippy also went missing in May 2021. So when this single African grey surfaced, both households claimed him.
For a while, Zazu stayed with Crystle. Then, in July 2023, Ntuli filed legal papers. After months of arguments and evidence, a magistrate ruled in 2024 that the bird should be returned to Ntuli. Crystle was forced to hand over Zazu — the parrot she had searched for, reunited with, and lived with again for three years. There is even footage of her final hour with him before the handover.
But the story isn’t finished. Crystle has appealed, and a cross-appeal is set for October 2025.
It’s not politics — it’s Polly-tics: two families parroting their case, feathers ruffled, one perch to stand on. For both Crystle and Obert, this is not just a pet — it’s family.
The case has also sparked bigger questions. African greys are among the most intelligent and long-lived birds on earth. They mimic human voices, form strong emotional bonds, and live for decades. Earlier this year in England, five African greys at Lincolnshire Wildlife Park had to be separated for swearing at visitors — a headline that shows how sharp and expressive they are. Experts here disagree on what proper care looks like: some warn about stress, self-plucking and even the danger of a single lick from a dog; the SPCA stresses freedom and enrichment.
South Africa is also at the centre of the global African grey trade. Tens of thousands are bred and exported every year, even as the species is listed as endangered in the wild. Mortality during transport, smuggling risks, and weak oversight all form part of the wider story.
So this begins with a missing “boy,” a miracle reunion, and a courtroom handover that broke a heart — but it grows into a story about welfare, ownership, and responsibility. It’s a human drama that will resonate with Carte Blanche viewers who see their own animals as family.
Polly doesn’t want a cracker — Polly wants a parent. Whose perch is it really — and what does this fight say about people and their parrot pets?
